title: Green Port Modernization and Operational Performance: A Structured Review of Developed- and Developing-Country Port Contexts
content: The modernization of a green port involves the replacement of equipment, the use of cleaner energy, digital coordination, adaptation of infrastructure and management practice change. Its value in operation is contingent on the extent to which these interventions respond to service constraints which may be identified and are feasible in local circumstances. This is a narrative review that organizes research from an annotated bibliography provided, with some appropriate official documents added. It analyzes through the lens of developed and developing nation port contexts in terms of throughput, vessel turnaround, operating cost per twenty-foot equivalent unit, congestion and service reliability. These are distinguished as environmental commitments, implementation assessments, stakeholder perceptions, modeled outcomes and documented performance changes. There are published studies that validate the linkage between green practices, organizational capability and performance, and these studies typically don't distinguish between the impacts of individual modernization investments. From Europe, Asia, Africa and South Asia, evidence shows that governance, financing, provision of electricity, maintenance, and coordination of hinterland conditions the implementation. Documentary illustrations from Los Angeles and Chattogram are provided to understand the need for different interpretations in emissions reporting, user assessments and project forecasts. A framework is developed that connects the decision appraisal, the implementation, intermediate operating changes and the separately assessed business and environmental outcomes. It suggests comparative research on decision episodes and longitudinal research with clear delineation of decisions, and clear accounting of costs, as well as explicit consideration of alternate explanations.
